questions.prompt: The eight planets can be sorted into two main families. What are they?
questions.explanation: The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small rocky worlds; the four outer planets are gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and ice giants (Uranus, Neptune).
questions.misconception: Sorting by temperature or color feels natural from pictures, but composition — what the planet is actually made of — is the real dividing line between the two families.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the smallest card — the smallest radius of the eight?
questions.explanation: Mercury is the smallest planet, with a radius of about 2,440 km — only 0.38 times Earth's. Pluto is smaller, but it is a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets.
questions.misconception: Mars is small in the solar system's story, but Mercury is smaller — and Pluto is not in the deck at all because it is a dwarf planet.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the shortest day of the eight?
questions.explanation: Jupiter spins the fastest of all the planets — one rotation, and therefore one day, takes only about 9.9 hours.
questions.misconception: It feels natural to assume the biggest planet spins slowest, but Jupiter is actually the fastest spinner in the solar system.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the longest year?
questions.explanation: Neptune, the most distant planet, takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun once — the longest year of the eight planets.
questions.misconception: Jupiter is the biggest, so it is easy to assume its year is longest too — but year length follows distance from the Sun, not size, and Neptune is farthest away.

questions.prompt: What does 'gas giant' mean for Jupiter and Saturn?
options: They are mostly hydrogen and helium with no solid surface near their clouds
They are made of frozen gas like a giant ice cube
They have rocky surfaces hidden under thin gas clouds
They are mostly empty gas with almost no mass
questions.explanation: Gas giants are composed overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium, like the Sun, and have no solid surface to stand on anywhere near their visible cloud tops.
questions.misconception: Some learners picture a 'gas giant' as a thin cloud ball that is mostly empty — in reality it is a vast, dense planet; the name refers to composition, not flimsiness.

questions.prompt: Why does every card use Earth as the reference for radius and gravity?
options: Because Earth is the biggest planet
So every number compares against the world you already know
Because Earth has the shortest year
questions.explanation: Writing sizes and gravity 'in Earths' (1 ×, 0.38 ×, 2.5 ×) gives every learner an immediate mental anchor — you know exactly what one Earth is.
questions.misconception: Earth is not the biggest or smallest planet — it is merely the reference we already live on, which is exactly why it makes the best measuring stick.
